extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, patent litigators, judges, and law students interested in remedies and empirical patent litigation studies
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating district court decisions on permanent injunctions in patent cases after the Supreme Court's eBay v. MercExchange decision. Focuses on how courts apply the four-factor equitable test and which factual/patent characteristics correlate with grants or denials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreparable harm (eBay factor 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patentee has demonstrated that it has suffered an irreparable injury such that monetary damages would be an inadequate remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The traditional presumption of irreparable harm following a finding of infringement 'did not survive' eBay; the patentee must demonstrate actual irreparable injury. Courts assess conduct inconsistent with defending the right to exclude (e.g., broad licensing or using patents to extract money rather than to exclude) as weighing against irreparable harm. Examples of harms courts have found sufficient include loss of market share, loss of goodwill, and price erosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate remedy at law (eBay factor 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether monetary damages provide an adequate remedy for the patentee's injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of a 'consistent desire to obtain royalties' or other licensing activity may show that money damages are adequate. Willingness to license the patent (especially nonexclusive or standard-rate licensing) commonly suggests the injury is compensable in money and weighs against an injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of hardships (eBay factor 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the balance of hardships between the patentee and infringer favors granting equitable relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider uncertainties such as the infringer's ability to design around, the possibility of patent invalidation in reexamination, and the economic harms to the infringer (e.g., losing customers if a product feature is removed). When hardships favor neither party, this factor may be neutral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest (eBay factor 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether entering an injunction would be in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts weigh public benefits from a strong patent system against harms from injunctions (e.g., when an injunction would unduly harm consumers or when the patentee seeks an injunction merely as a bargaining chip). In some cases the public interest favors a liability rule (damages) rather than an injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of irreparable harm abolished post-eBay
rubrics_metrics.description: The pre-eBay practice of presuming irreparable harm from a finding of infringement no longer obtains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-eBay courts require plaintiffs to carry the burden of establishing irreparable injury based on traditional equitable principles; mere finding of infringement (even willful infringement) does not automatically trigger an injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee business model / licensing activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patentee has licensed or offered to license the patented technology to others (including nonexclusive licensing) and its overall licensing practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensing activity can indicate both a lack of irreparable harm and the existence of an adequate remedy at law. Courts often view consistent licensing or use of patents 'as a sword to extract money' as weighing against injunctive relief, though some empirical reports find injunctions still granted in many licensed cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicing entity vs. non-practicing entity (PAE) status
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patentee practices the patent in the marketplace or is primarily a licensing/assertion entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies and court decisions show PAEs (non-practicing entities) are significantly less likely to obtain injunctions post-eBay; practicing patentees receive injunctions at markedly higher rates. Justice Kennedy's concurrence influenced courts to treat non-practicing patentees with skepticism regarding injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of the parties / direct competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patentee and accused infringer are direct competitors in the same market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parties are competitors, courts are much more likely to find irreparable harm and to grant injunctions. The existence of direct marketplace competition has been described as the single most important determinant of whether an injunction will issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-component / multicomponent-product consideration (holdup risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patented invention is only a small component of a larger, multicomponent infringing product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Kennedy suggested that injunctions may be inappropriate where the patented feature is a small component because of holdup concerns. Empirical scholarship indicates courts frequently deny injunctions in such situations; courts have not awarded injunctions where the patent covers only a small component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement as a consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the infringer's conduct was willful and whether that should affect equitable relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Willfulness has traditionally been relevant to equitable relief and can favor injunctions, but empirical evidence is mixed: some courts grant injunctions against willful infringers while others deny them, and scholarship finds willfulness is not consistently predictive of injunction outcomes post-eBay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidentiary harms courts find persuasive
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific factual showings that courts have considered sufficient to establish irreparable harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have cited loss of market share, loss of customer goodwill, and price erosion as types of harms supporting irreparable injury. Demonstrating that licensing practices or failure to enforce rights undermine exclusivity can undercut these showings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-level characteristics as possible predictors
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes of the patents at issue (e.g., number of claims, prior-art citation counts, technological field) may correlate with injunction outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This article notes prior empirical work finding patent characteristics predictive of patent value and litigation likelihood; the study seeks to test whether such characteristics correlate with districts' injunction decisions, recognizing omitted-variable concerns in earlier work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural and dataset inclusion/exclusion rules for studying injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Which judicial decisions should be included when empirically studying permanent injunctions after eBay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author included contested permanent injunction decisions by federal district courts from May 13, 2006 through Dec. 31, 2013 and excluded uncontested injunctions (default or consent), preliminary injunctions (different legal test), and design patent cases. Uncontested injunctions were excluded because they skew grant rates and provide little reasoning for analysis.
